analysis.one_liner: Narrows federal clean-water protections and pays landowners double for any property value loss.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee in November 2021, it never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would sharply shrink which waters the federal government can protect under the Clean Water Act. Only rivers, lakes, and oceans that are navigable or connected to navigable waters would count; most wetlands, intermittent streams, drainage channels, and groundwater would be dropped from federal oversight and left to the states. It would also bar the EPA and Army Corps from ever issuing new rules defining protected waters without a new act of Congress, require federal officials to get written consent before collecting water data on private land, and pay landowners twice the value of any property loss caused by a federal water rule — with the rule not taking effect until every landowner claimant is paid. The bill was never taken up by the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and developers of land containing wetlands or intermittent streams, who would no longer need federal permits to fill or build on them, and industries whose discharges would fall outside federal permitting. Large landowners would also gain a new entitlement: double payment from federal agency budgets for any property value loss caused by a water rule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, large landowners, and discharging industries

how_it_helps.text: The bill would remove most wetlands without a continuous surface connection to protected waters, intermittent and ephemeral channels, and drainage structures from the definition of federally protected 'navigable waters.'
It would bar the EPA from using the 'significant nexus' test — the method courts used to decide whether smaller waters affect larger protected ones — and declare groundwater entirely a state matter.

It would nullify the 1986 Corps regulatory rule and the 2008 post-Rapanos jurisdictional guidance, and prohibit the EPA and the Corps from issuing any new rule or guidance on the definition of protected waters unless Congress expressly authorizes it.
Federal representatives could collect water-quality information on private land only with the owner's written consent, with the owner present if they choose.

If a federal water regulation reduces a property's fair market value or economic viability, the issuing agency would pay the owner twice the loss, from its own operating budget, and the regulation would have no force until every landowner claimant was compensated.

analysis.who_pays: Downstream communities, whose drinking water and fisheries depend on the wetlands and intermittent streams the bill would strip from federal protection, and taxpayers, who would fund the double-compensation payments through agency operating budgets. Weaker federal standards would also shift water-quality disputes to a patchwork of state rules of varying strength.

drawbacks.text: Millions of acres of wetlands and intermittent streams that filter pollution and feed drinking-water sources would lose federal protection; water bodies that flow only part of the year still carry pollution to rivers people rely on.

The compensation clause would make new federal water rules practically impossible: a rule would have no effect until every landowner with a claim was paid double, from money the agency needs for its normal operations.

Honest supporters' point is real: federal permitting and jurisdictional determinations can impose genuine costs and uncertainty on property owners, including smaller ones, and the bill addresses that with consent requirements and fast judicial review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The legitimate concern — that federal water jurisdiction has been uncertain and burdensome for landowners since the Rapanos decision — is addressed in ways that go far beyond it. The core of the bill removes federal protection from a large share of the nation's waters and puts a mechanism in place (double compensation, paid from agency budgets, required before any rule takes effect) that would prevent future Congresses and agencies from extending protection at all. The benefit to landowners is real but narrow; the cost falls broadly on water quality and the public's ability to set national standards.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day it was introduced, moved to a subcommittee the next day, and never received a hearing, a markup, or any vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Rouzer introduced the bill on November 3, 2021.
It was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day, and to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment the following day.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded before the end of the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyone who relies on existing federal clean-water protections is better off that the bill died, since its compensation mechanism alone would have made future federal water rules nearly unenforceable. No one gained materially from the outcome.

for.name: Rep. David Rouzer
for.role: Sponsor, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; it advanced no further under his leadership.

against.name: Chair Peter DeFazio

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the last recorded action was a subcommittee referral on November 4, 2021.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got to a vote, so no vote breakdown exists; it had one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: Land containing wetlands or seasonal streams would no longer need federal Section 404 permits to fill or build, cutting cost and delay. The cost is borne downstream: those same wetlands and streams filter pollution and feed drinking-water supplies.

Drainage channels, intermittent flows, and non-abutting wetlands would be explicitly excluded from federal jurisdiction, and the bill preserves existing agricultural exemptions. Public cost is reduced federal oversight of farm runoff reaching protected waters.

Fewer waters under federal jurisdiction means fewer discharge permits, smaller jurisdictional determinations, and a ban on the significant nexus test that had extended federal review. The gain comes at the expense of downstream water quality.

industries.industry: EPA and Army Corps (federal water regulators)
industries.note: The agencies would lose jurisdiction over most wetlands and seasonal waters, be barred from issuing any new definitional rules without an act of Congress, need written landowner consent to collect data, and pay double the value of any regulatory loss out of their own operating budgets.
